vignette: Vikram's hands still remember the weight of his rifle long before his boots hit the concrete floor of the distribution center, but at seventy-nine, the metal has long been traded for a clip board. Divorced after forty years, he lives alone in a quiet house whose doors he keeps locked not out of habit but out of a quiet, settled conviction that the outside world remains fundamentally unpredictable. He does not speak often of his years in uniform, but when he does, the memory does not arrive as a distant story. It arrives as a sudden, breathless narrowing of the present. He had come to believe that safety was an illusion maintained only through constant vigilance, a certainty that settled into him during the campaign when a sudden shift in terrain had turned routine patrol into an ambush, and the crack of gunfire, the dust choking his lungs, and the desperate scramble for cover rewired his understanding of how quickly life could be taken. That moment did not stay in the past; it taught his mind to scan for threats, to brace before a sound fully registered, to interpret sudden movements as imminent danger. Over the decades, this scanning became automatic. He began avoiding crowded spaces not because he disliked people, but because the unpredictability of crowds felt like a return to that open ground, and he learned that stepping away from noise, from groups, from unexpected conversations kept the tension at bay. The avoidance settled in slowly, week by week, then year by year, until the house grew quieter, his social circle thinned, and his days narrowed to routines that felt controllable. Now, at the warehouse, that narrow routine is constantly tested. The facility is a maze of high shelving units, concrete aisles, and the rhythmic hiss of pneumatic doors opening and closing. Vikram works the receiving dock, a role he chose specifically for its predictable flow, but predictability here is fragile. When a forklift backfires with a sharp metallic pop, his shoulders hike, his breath catches, and for a few seconds he is back in that valley, certain the ground will shake and the next round will find him. What frightens him most is not the noise itself, but the way his body betrays him by responding as though he is still unprotected, still unarmed, still exposed. He has learned to stand slightly away from the loading bays, to time his breaks when the machinery cycles down, to excuse himself when the supervisors raise their voices over the radio, because proximity to sudden sounds and authoritative commands triggers a reflexive readiness to flee. He avoids these moments not out of defiance, but because he knows that staying forces his nervous system to relive the ambush, and the recovery takes hours. Over the years, this pattern has hardened into a quiet architecture of daily life. He arrives early, leaves early, skips the staff lunches, and speaks only when necessary, because each interaction carries the unspoken risk of the unexpected, and each avoidance brings a fleeting, temporary relief that only deepens the isolation. The isolation has grown heavy. At seventy-nine, the weight of a life carefully narrowed feels less like protection and more like a slow erosion of what remains. He stopped going to the veterans' hall three years ago because the sudden laughter and overlapping conversations triggered a panic he could no longer dismiss as age or tiredness. His former marriage had quietly unraveled under the same weight; he had come to believe that his wife would eventually tire of his silence, and his attempts to keep her at arm's length to spare her his "fragility" only pushed her further away. Now, at work, the loop tightens with every shift. The forklift's beep pulls his attention inward, the memory of the ambush flares, his appraisal that the present moment is indistinguishable from the past takes hold, his body braces for threat, and his instinct to withdraw from the aisle reinforces the certainty that the world remains unsafe. He knows this pattern is costing him the rest of his life. He finally walked into the clinic last week not because he could no longer work, but because the quiet in his house had grown too loud, and the certainty that he would spend his remaining years bracing for a war that ended decades ago no longer felt manageable. He hopes, more than anything, to find a way to stop the bracing, to let the present moment be just a moment, and to live without waiting for the next explosion.
